props.title: Poor Pretty Eddie
props.initialSlug: Nowhere to run, nowhere to hide.

sections.content: **Poor Pretty Eddie** (1975) stands as one of the most disturbing entries in the Southern Gothic exploitation genre, blending elements of Deliverance (1972) and **The Texas Chain Saw Massacre** (1974). This fever dream of a film follows Leslie Uggams as a famous singer stranded at a backwoods Georgia motor lodge where she's terrorized by Eddie (Michael Christian), a delusional Elvis wannabe. The film's unsettling atmosphere and controversial themes made it notorious on the drive-in circuit, where it was also released under titles like "Black Vengeance" and "Heartbreak Motel."

sections.content: The film fits into a specific 1970s movement of Southern exploitation films that explored post-Civil Rights tensions through horror. Like **Walking Tall** (1973) and **Macon County Line** (1974), it uses genre elements to address racial and cultural divisions. Director Chris Robinson and cinematographer David Worth create a hallucinatory visual style that would influence later Southern Gothic films like **Angel Heart** (1987). SUBHEAD: Impact on Rural Horror

**Poor Pretty Eddie** (1975) helped establish tropes that would become staples of the rural horror subgenre: isolated locations, cultural clash between urban and rural characters, and themes of degradation. These elements appear in later films like **The Beyond** (1981) and **House of 1000 Corpses** (2003), showing how the film's DNA spread through horror cinema.
